definition: Components at odd whole-number multiples of a fundamental frequency, such as the third, fifth and seventh harmonics. Symmetric clipping of a sine creates odd harmonics; asymmetric nonlinearities can also produce even harmonics.
example: A clipped 1 kHz note puts odd harmonics at 3, 5 and 7 kHz into the tweeter.

definition: A small amplifier designed to drive headphones, which need far less power than speakers but vary from about 16 Ω to several hundred ohms. It should have low output impedance.
example: 10 mW needs 0.57 V into 32 Ω but 1.73 V into 300 Ω.

definition: The household AC electricity supply. Contact with live mains conductors or charged internal circuits can be fatal. Do not open or modify mains-powered amplifiers for these lessons; use external low-voltage connections within equipment instructions.
example: A power amplifier's mains wiring and supply capacitors can be lethal.

definition: The SI unit of power: one joule per second. Amplifier output and speaker power ratings are in watts.
example: 28.3 V RMS into 8 Ω is about 100 W.

definition: The connected chain of microphones, DI boxes, mixer, processing, amplifiers and loudspeakers that brings sources to listeners at the right level and balance.
example: A pub gig's sound system might be a small mixer and two powered speakers.

definition: A public address system: the loudspeakers, amplifiers and processing that reproduce sound for an audience. In live music, "the PA" usually means the main speaker system.
example: A festival PA has line-array mains, subwoofers and delay towers.

definition: The level of background noise in a system or device with no signal. Signals must stay well above it.
example: Equivalent input noise is a preamp noise specification referred to its input; it is not automatically the noise level at the output.

definition: A device that combines many inputs into a few outputs with independent level, tone, routing and effects control for each.
example: A 16-channel mixing console might feed main L/R, four monitor mixes and two effects.

definition: Digital audio workstation: software for recording, editing, processing and mixing audio, often with MIDI facilities. Routing and mixer features depend on the application.
example: Ableton Live's mixer has sends, returns and groups like a console.

definition: One input channel's controls on a mixer, usually in order: preamp gain, high-pass filter, insert, EQ, dynamics, aux sends, pan, fader and routing.
example: Each microphone gets its own channel strip.

definition: The control at the top of a channel strip that sets how much the preamp amplifies the incoming signal. It sets the channel's signal-to-noise ratio and headroom.
example: Set the trim with the singer at full voice.

definition: A send-and-return connection that loops a channel's signal out to an external processor and back, in series with the channel.
example: Patch a hardware compressor into the vocal channel's insert point.

definition: Adjusting the level of particular frequency ranges with filters (shelving, parametric, graphic) to shape tone, fix problems or make room for other sources.
example: Cutting 300 Hz on a muddy guitar is EQ.

definition: An EQ that boosts or cuts everything above (high shelf) or below (low shelf) a corner frequency by a set amount.
example: A −3 dB high shelf at 2 kHz is a baffle-step-style correction.

definition: An EQ band whose centre frequency, gain and bandwidth (Q) can all be set, for precise boosts or cuts.
example: A narrow parametric cut at 2.5 kHz removes a feedback ring.

definition: Processing that changes level according to the signal's own level: compressors, limiters, gates and expanders.
example: Many digital desks have a gate and compressor on every channel.

definition: A dynamics processor that reduces the level of a signal above a set threshold by a chosen ratio, narrowing its dynamic range.
example: A 4:1 compressor turns 8 dB over threshold into 2 dB over.

definition: A dynamics processor that mutes or strongly reduces a signal when it falls below a threshold, removing spill and noise between notes.
example: A gate on a tom mic cuts the cymbal spill between hits.

definition: A control that sends an adjustable copy of a channel to a separate aux bus, used for monitor mixes and effects. Sends can be pre- or post-fader.
example: Aux 1 feeds the singer's wedge; aux 5 feeds the reverb.

definition: Taken before the channel fader, so the send level does not change when the fader moves. Used for monitor mixes.
example: A pre-fader monitor send stays the same when the FOH engineer rides the vocal.

definition: Taken after the channel fader, so the send follows fader moves. Used for effects like reverb, so wet and dry stay in proportion.
example: Pull the vocal fader down and its post-fader reverb send fades too.

definition: A separate mix sent to the performers so they can hear themselves, through floor wedges, side fills or in-ear monitors. Usually fed from pre-fader aux sends.
example: The drummer's monitor mix is mostly kick, bass and click.

definition: Placing a mono signal between the left and right of a stereo mix with the pan control.
example: Panning a synth pad 30% left makes room for a guitar on the right.

definition: A sliding level control on a mixer, setting a channel's or bus's level in the mix. Its unity mark (0 dB) passes the signal unchanged.
example: Keep faders near 0 dB so there is travel both ways.

definition: Choosing where a signal goes: which buses, groups and outputs a channel feeds.
example: Route all drum channels to subgroup 1.

definition: A point in a mixer where several signals are summed, such as the main L/R mix, an aux bus or a subgroup.
example: The main stereo bus feeds the PA.

definition: A bus that sums related channels (all drums, all backing vocals) to one fader, so a section can be controlled or processed together.
example: Compress the whole drum subgroup with one compressor.

definition: A control group where one master fader remotely sets the levels of member channels without summing their audio. Named after the voltage-controlled amplifiers that did this in analogue desks.
example: Pull the drums VCA down 3 dB and every drum channel drops 3 dB.

definition: The digital-console equivalent of a VCA group: one fader controls the levels of member channels without summing audio.
example: A DCA for backing vocals lets you ride all three singers at once.

definition: Setting the level at each stage of a signal chain so the signal stays well above the noise floor and well below clipping everywhere.
example: Good gain staging starts with the preamp, not the master fader.

definition: A gain of 1 (0 dB): output equals input.
example: Set outboard gear to unity so it neither boosts nor cuts.

definition: External hardware processors (compressors, EQs, effects) connected to a mixer, outside the console itself.
example: A rack of outboard gear patched into the inserts.

definition: How far a signal is above the noise floor, in decibels. Higher is cleaner.
example: A signal at +4 dBu over a −86 dBu noise floor has a 90 dB signal-to-noise ratio.

definition: Decibels relative to a specified digital full-scale reference. For integer sample-peak metering, zero dBFS is the largest representable sample magnitude; floating-point internal signals and reconstructed true peaks require their stated conventions.
example: Nominal levels around −18 dBFS leave headroom for peaks.

definition: Voltage level in decibels relative to 0.775 V RMS. Professional line level is +4 dBu (about 1.23 V RMS).
Voltage level in decibels relative to 1 V RMS. Consumer line level is −10 dBV (about 0.32 V RMS); dBu = dBV + about 2.2 dB.
example: −44.5 dBV is about −42.3 dBu.

definition: The normal signal level a piece of equipment is designed to work at, leaving headroom above it.
example: A pro console's nominal level is +4 dBu.

definition: A box that converts an instrument or line-level signal into a low-impedance, balanced, mic-level signal for a mixer's mic input, usually with a ground lift and pad.
example: Check source output, DI input headroom and destination input; use a suitable line input directly when appropriate.

definition: A DI box using only a transformer, needing no power. The transformer gives galvanic isolation.
example: A passive DI suits a synth's low-impedance line output.

definition: A DI box with a buffer amplifier powered by phantom power or a battery. It loads high-impedance sources such as passive guitar pickups very lightly.
example: Compare the actual DI input impedance and headroom with the instrument’s output rather than assuming every active DI is better.

definition: An audio interconnection feature that changes a signal-shield or audio-reference path to reduce hum from a loop. The exact circuit varies and can preserve a phantom-power return; it must never mean disconnecting protective mains earth.
example: Follow the DI manufacturer’s switch instructions; do not modify mains earth wiring.

definition: An unwanted current path when equipment is connected to ground at more than one point, which can induce mains hum in audio.
example: A synth and a mixer on different power sockets can form a ground loop.

definition: Separating two circuits so no direct current can flow between them, while the signal still passes (for example through a transformer).
example: A passive DI's transformer gives galvanic isolation between stage and desk.

definition: Two coils on a shared core that pass an AC signal by magnetic coupling, changing its voltage and impedance and isolating the two sides.
example: A DI transformer steps a line-level signal down to mic level.

definition: An amplifier with high input impedance and low output impedance, used to stop a sensitive source being loaded down.
example: An active DI's buffer stops a passive pickup losing treble.

definition: The impedance presented by a device input to its source, potentially varying with frequency. A sufficiently high input impedance relative to that source reduces loading; the appropriate value depends on the source.
example: Input impedance and a source’s output impedance are different specifications.

definition: A bundle of many balanced audio lines in one cable, usually with a stage box of connectors, linking the stage to the mixer.
example: A 32-channel multicore runs 50 m to front of house.

definition: The audience side of a venue. The FOH engineer mixes there, and the FOH (main) speakers cover the audience.
example: The FOH mixer sits in the middle of the audience.

definition: A line of loudspeaker elements designed to control coverage through their spacing, directivity and processing. Some frequency and distance ranges approximate line-source spreading; all finite arrays eventually require far-field analysis.
example: Do not apply a universal three-decibel-per-doubling rule across every array, frequency or distance.

definition: A sound source small enough, or far enough away, to radiate as if from a single point, so level falls 6 dB per doubling of distance.
example: A single PA box behaves like a point source in its far field.

definition: An arrangement of several subwoofers, using spacing, delays or polarity changes, to shape low-frequency coverage. Cardioid and end-fire arrays cancel sound behind them (towards the stage); arc arrays spread coverage more evenly across a wide audience.
example: An end-fire array of four subs can be much quieter on stage than out front.

definition: Earphones carrying a performer’s monitor mix through a wired or wireless system. Removing a wedge from that mix removes its loudspeaker-to-microphone path, but in-ear levels still need control to protect hearing.
example: In-ear monitoring removes the wedge-to-microphone path only when the wedge is removed from that mix; excessive earphone level can still damage hearing.

definition: Speakers at the side of the stage that give performers a general monitor mix across the stage area.
example: Side fills let the band hear each other across a wide stage.

definition: Small speakers along the stage lip covering the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage.
example: Front fills stop the first rows hearing only the stage sound.

definition: A speaker placed further back in a large venue to restore level, fed with an electronic delay so its sound lines up with the arrival from the main speakers.
example: With a 40 m path difference, a delay speaker needs about 117 ms of delay.

definition: The time delay a device or process adds between input and output, such as digital processing or a converter.
example: Use the actual processor’s specified or measured latency; block duration alone does not establish end-to-end latency.

definition: Loudspeakers suspended above the stage or audience with rigging, rather than on stands or the floor.
example: Line arrays are usually flown above each side of the stage.

definition: The howl or squeal when sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone, is amplified, and comes out louder, repeatedly. It occurs at frequencies where loop gain reaches 0 dB in reinforcing phase.
example: Pointing a vocal mic at a wedge invites acoustic feedback.

definition: The total gain around the path speaker → air → microphone → amplifier → speaker. If it reaches 1 (0 dB) at a frequency with reinforcing phase, the system feeds back.
example: Halving the mic-to-source distance lets you drop loop gain by 6 dB.

definition: How much gain a sound system can use before it starts to feed back. Increased by close miking, directional mics, fewer open mics and good speaker placement.
example: Placing a wedge near the appropriate microphone-pattern null can improve the available margin; measure the actual system rather than assuming a fixed gain.

definition: Potential acoustic gain is an approximate geometry-and-microphone-count model of usable amplification before feedback. Needed acoustic gain estimates what the audience requires; their comparison is useful planning evidence rather than an exact stability proof.
example: If the approximate potential gain is below the estimated needed gain, change geometry, microphone count or coverage rather than assuming extra electronic gain can solve the shortfall.

definition: How many microphones are live at once. Each doubling of similarly coupled open mics costs about 3 dB of gain before feedback (10 × log10 of the count).
example: Muting unused mics on a panel discussion adds feedback margin.

definition: Finding a system's feedback frequencies by slowly raising gain until it starts to ring, then cutting each with a narrow EQ.
example: Ringing out the wedges before soundcheck found a problem at 630 Hz.

definition: A very narrow filter that deeply cuts one frequency. Feedback suppressors place notch filters automatically on feedback frequencies.
example: A feedback suppressor typically adds only a few dB of margin.

definition: A studio speaker designed for listening from about 1–2 m, so you hear more direct sound and less room. Not to be confused with the acoustic near field.
example: A pair of 5-inch near-field monitors on stands behind the desk.

definition: A loudspeaker containing its own power amplifier. Many use active or DSP crossovers, but a powered speaker can also contain a passive crossover and can use mains, batteries or another specified supply.
example: Most home-studio monitors are powered speakers.

definition: A standing-wave resonance of a room at a frequency where whole numbers of half-wavelengths fit between surfaces. Modes make the bass at your seat boom at some frequencies and vanish at others.
example: A 5 m-long room has its first axial mode at 34.3 Hz.

definition: In an ideal rigid rectangular room, axial modes vary along one coordinate and involve one pair of opposite surfaces; tangential modes involve two pairs, and oblique modes all three. Their actual prominence depends on source/listener positions and damping.
example: The (1,0,0) mode is axial; (1,1,0) is tangential; (1,1,1) is oblique.

definition: In a standing-wave pattern, a pressure node is a position of zero acoustic-pressure variation for that mode and an antinode is a position of maximum variation. Ideal rigid rectangular-room corners are pressure antinodes of the modal families, while general wall positions can still have nodes along another coordinate.
example: A node of the first length mode at the midpoint does not imply zero total sound at that seat.

definition: A direction or position where a signal largely cancels: the rear of a cardioid mic, the side of a dipole, or a room position at a mode's pressure node.
example: Aim a mic's null at the monitor wedge.

definition: The frequency above which room modes overlap so densely that the room behaves statistically, estimated as about 2000 × √(RT60/V). Below it, treat the room as modes; above it, as reflections and reverberation.
example: A 43 m³ control room with 0.44 s RT60 has a Schroeder frequency of about 200 Hz.

definition: The dense, decaying sound of many reflections that continues after a source stops. Its length is measured as RT60.
example: A cathedral's reverberation lasts several seconds.

definition: The time corresponding to a sixty-decibel decay of sound level after a source stops, commonly reported by frequency band. Control-room decay targets depend on room size and the applicable design guidance.
example: A treated 43 m³ room might have RT60 ≈ 0.44 s.

definition: Wallace Sabine's empirical formula from around 1900: RT60 = 0.161 × V / A, with V the room volume in m³ and A the total absorption in metric sabins. It assumes a fairly live room with diffuse sound.
example: Raising a 43.2 m³ room's absorption from about 7.7 to 15.7 metric sabins roughly halves its RT60, from 0.9 s to 0.44 s.

definition: A statistical reverberation model that accounts differently for higher average absorption than Sabine’s formula. It still needs an adequately diffuse field and suitable absorption distribution; a small non-diffuse booth is not automatically well modelled.
example: Check the model assumptions rather than choosing Eyring solely because a room sounds dry.

definition: The unit of sound absorption: one metric sabin is the absorption of 1 m² of a perfect absorber. Total absorption A = sum of each surface's area × its absorption coefficient.
example: 10 m² of panels with α = 0.9 give 9 metric sabins.

definition: A range of frequencies one octave wide (the top is twice the bottom), such as the band centred on 125 Hz. Acoustic data like absorption and RT60 are given per band. Third-octave bands split each octave into three narrower bands for finer detail.
example: A panel's α may be 0.2 in the 125 Hz band and 0.95 at 1 kHz.

definition: A doubling (or halving) of frequency.
example: 110 Hz to 220 Hz is one octave.

definition: Material or a device that converts sound energy to heat, reducing reflections and reverberation.
example: Absorbers at the first-reflection points tighten a monitor's stereo image.

definition: An absorber such as mineral wool, fibreglass or thick foam that absorbs by friction as air moves through it. Most effective where air velocity is high, about a quarter wavelength from a hard wall.
example: A 10 cm porous absorber is effective in the mids and highs but weak in the bass.

definition: Fibrous insulation made from rock or glass, widely used as a porous acoustic absorber. Cover it, because loose fibres irritate skin and lungs.
example: 100 mm mineral-wool panels are a common DIY absorber.

definition: The local oscillatory velocity of the medium’s particles, distinct from the propagation speed of sound. For normal incidence on an ideal rigid wall, the normal component is zero at the wall and has standing-wave antinodes a quarter wavelength away.
example: A porous absorber spaced off the wall sits where particle velocity is higher.

definition: Resistance to airflow through a porous specimen, expressed as pressure difference divided by volume flow rate or, for specific flow resistance, by face velocity. Flow resistivity is specific flow resistance divided by material thickness; compare only values with the same definition and units.
example: Do not compare flow resistance and flow resistivity as though they were the same numerical property.

definition: A surface shaped to scatter sound in many directions without removing much energy, breaking up strong reflections while keeping a room live. Effective mainly at mid and high frequencies.
example: A wooden diffuser on the back wall of a control room.

definition: A rapid series of repeats from sound bouncing between two parallel hard surfaces, heard as a ringing buzz after a clap.
example: Clap between bare parallel walls to hear flutter echo.

definition: An absorber designed to work at low frequencies: either a thick porous absorber (often in corners) or a tuned membrane or Helmholtz absorber.
example: Floor-to-ceiling bass traps in the front corners reduce modal peaks.

definition: A tuned low-frequency absorber excited by sound pressure: membrane or panel designs use a moving sheet over an air space, while Helmholtz designs use moving air in a neck or opening coupled to a cavity. Losses dissipate energy around resonance. Placement near pressure maxima can help; useful bandwidth depends on the design.
example: A membrane absorber tuned to 60 Hz tames a strong room mode.

definition: Reflected arrivals shortly after direct sound. Their levels, directions, spectrum and delays determine comb filtering and perceived imaging effects; an early reflection is not inherently detrimental in every listening purpose.
example: The desk surface often produces a strong early reflection.

definition: A way to find first-reflection points: sit at the listening position while someone slides a mirror along the wall; wherever you see a monitor's tweeter, put absorption.
example: The mirror trick found reflection points 1.2 m along each side wall.

definition: The standard stereo monitoring layout: the two speakers and the listener's head at the corners of an equilateral triangle, 60° apart.
example: Monitors 1.2 m apart need the listener 1.2 m from each.

definition: The line from a speaker along which its response is specified, usually between tweeter and woofer or as the manual states. It should point at the listener's ears.
example: Tilt the monitors so their acoustic axis meets ear height.

definition: Cancellation dips caused when a speaker's sound reflects off a nearby wall and returns out of phase. The first notch is near c/(4d) for a wall distance d.
example: A monitor 0.6 m from the front wall has its first SBIR notch near 143 Hz.

definition: Building speakers into a wall so their front is flush with it, removing the rear reflection that causes SBIR and baffle step.
example: Big studio main monitors are often flush-mounted.

definition: A Finnish maker of studio monitors whose monitor-placement guide is a widely used reference for setting up near-field monitors.
example: Genelec suggests less than 60 cm from monitor to front wall.

definition: Free room-acoustics measurement software by John Mulcahy for Windows, macOS and Linux. It measures frequency response, impulse response, waterfalls and RT60, and can calculate EQ filters.
example: Use REW with a calibrated USB mic to see your room's modes.

definition: A microphone with a characterised response for measurement. Many room-measurement models are omnidirectional and supplied with frequency-response calibration data; absolute SPL calibration and orientation still need the specified method.
example: A USB measurement mic plugs straight into a laptop running REW.

definition: A device that produces a precise known sound pressure, often 94 dB SPL (1 Pa) at 1 kHz, to check a sound level meter or measurement mic.
example: Check your meter reads 94.0 dB on the calibrator before measuring.

definition: Universal Serial Bus: the standard computer connection for peripherals, including audio interfaces and USB measurement microphones.
example: A USB measurement mic needs no separate audio interface.

definition: A test signal that glides smoothly through all frequencies. Recording it lets software calculate the impulse response with good noise rejection.
example: REW plays a swept sine from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

definition: For a linear time-invariant system, its output in response to an ideal unit impulse. It determines the system’s transfer function; practical swept-sine measurements estimate a response under stated conditions.
example: A room's impulse response shows each reflection as a spike after the direct sound.

definition: A 3D plot of frequency response over time as sound decays, showing which frequencies ring on. Room modes appear as long ridges.
example: A ridge at 47 Hz lasting 500 ms on the waterfall is a ringing mode.

definition: The room in a studio where engineers monitor and mix, treated for accurate listening.
example: A control room's RT60 is typically much shorter than a living room's.

definition: The seat where the engineer listens, ideally at the apex of the stereo triangle and away from the room's exact middle.
example: Genelec suggests the listening position be in the front part of the room.

definition: A logarithmic unit comparing two levels: 10 × log10 of a power ratio, or 20 × log10 of a voltage or pressure ratio. +6 dB is about double the pressure; +3 dB double the power.
example: +20 dB means ten times the voltage or pressure.

definition: The SI unit of frequency: one cycle per second. 1 kHz is 1000 Hz.
example: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

definition: The SI unit of resistance and impedance. Speakers are typically labelled 4, 8 or 16 Ω.
example: An 8 Ω speaker on 28.3 V RMS draws 3.5 A.

definition: The SI unit of electrical potential difference (voltage).
example: Professional line level is about 1.23 V RMS.

definition: The SI unit of electric current.
example: 100 W into 8 Ω needs about 3.5 A RMS.

definition: One thousandth of a second. Sound travels about 34 cm in 1 ms.
example: A 40 m path difference is about 117 ms.

definition: One millionth of a second.
example: A 2 cm driver offset is about 58 µs.

definition: The SI unit of absolute temperature: 0 K is absolute zero and 0 °C = 273.15 K. The speed of sound depends on absolute temperature.
The Greek capital letter sigma, meaning "add up all of these".
example: A = Σ S × α means add every surface's area times its absorption coefficient.

definition: The symbol meaning "approximately equal to": the result has been rounded or relies on an approximation.
Two quantities are proportional when one is always a fixed multiple of the other, so if one doubles, so does the other. In formulas it is written with the symbol ∝.
example: Pressure ∝ 1/r means double the distance gives half the pressure.

definition: The Greek capital letter delta, usually meaning "change in" or "difference between".
example: ΔL = 6 dB means the level changed by 6 dB.

definition: The span between the quietest and loudest levels a system can handle, such as from self-noise to maximum SPL.
example: A mic with 12 dB-A self-noise and 117 dB max SPL has about 105 dB of dynamic range.

definition: Electric current with a nonzero component that does not alternate direction; in steady circuit calculations DC refers to time-independent quantities. DC voltage is a constant potential difference, while a DC component is the zero-frequency or mean part of a signal.
example: A multimeter measures a speaker's DC resistance, about 6 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver.

definition: The distance a wave travels during one cycle: the speed of sound divided by the frequency. Audible wavelengths in air range from about 17 m at 20 Hz to 1.7 cm at 20 kHz.
example: A 100 Hz tone has a wavelength of about 3.4 m.

definition: A person who plays recorded music for an audience, often through a PA with heavy bass content.
example: DJ sets in clubs often push subwoofers hard below 40 Hz.

definition: Earplugs or ear defenders worn to reduce the sound level reaching the ears. Under Great Britain's noise regulations it must be made available at the lower action value and worn at the upper one.
example: Musicians' earplugs are hearing protection that keeps the band's balance while lowering the level.

definition: A family of ported-box alignments from Thiele's tables (QB3 is the best known) whose bass response is close to, but not exactly, a Butterworth shape. They suit drivers with a lower Qts than a true Butterworth ported alignment needs.
example: Box-modelling software can show a QB3 alignment as one option for a low-Qts woofer.

definition: The Greek letter rho. This module uses it for air density in the compliance-volume model and for electrical resistivity in the cable model; these are different quantities with different units.
example: The cable example assumes 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ ohm-metres; use actual material and temperature data for a real wire.

definition: An amplifier whose gain is set by a control voltage rather than a knob. In a synth an envelope drives a VCA to shape each note's loudness; analogue mixing consoles use them so one VCA-group fader can control several channels.
example: Pulling a console's VCA master down 6 dB lowers every assigned channel by 6 dB.

definition: An ideal statistical sound field with approximately uniform average energy density and energy arriving equally from all directions. It is an assumption of simple reverberation models; a reflected field is not automatically diffuse.

Assessing sound exposure and the risk of hearing harm, then selecting controls and further action under the applicable requirements. Workplace assessment considers both time-averaged exposure and peaks.
The angular region of strongest acoustic output from a source or driver combination. Other lobes and nulls can appear because different contributions interfere.
The part of a power amplifier that drives the load with the required voltage and current. Conduction class, losses, current capability and protection depend on the actual circuit.

An amplifier output designed to drive headphones under stated load conditions. Available voltage, current, output impedance and the headphones’ sensitivity and impedance jointly determine level and response.

A loudspeaker used as a reference for recording or mixing decisions. Its specified listening distance, acoustic axis and placement guidance depend on the model; not every studio monitor is a near-field design.
The shield contact of a conventional three-pin balanced microphone XLR connection. In standard phantom powering it provides the DC return; follow the equipment’s actual wiring instructions.

The positive-polarity signal contact of a conventional three-pin balanced microphone XLR. Standard phantom power applies DC to this contact through a feed resistor; it is not the shield contact of a five-pin MIDI DIN socket.

The negative-polarity signal contact of a conventional three-pin balanced microphone XLR. In standard phantom powering it receives the same DC supply arrangement as XLR pin 2; actual equipment wiring must still be checked.

A mechanical or acoustic element that stores energy when displaced or compressed and produces a restoring force. In a small-signal loudspeaker model, the suspension and the air in a sealed box both act as springs.
A property describing inertia: how strongly an object resists acceleration, measured in kilograms. A driver’s moving mass and restoring compliance jointly determine its ideal resonance.
A device that converts mechanical motion into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. A moving voice coil can act as a generator and produce back electromotive force.

A loudspeaker aimed towards performers so they can hear a monitor mix on stage. A floor wedge is a common form; its placement relative to a microphone’s pickup pattern affects feedback. The loudspeaker and the monitor mix feeding it are different things.
example: Feed the singer’s floor wedge from a suitable aux mix, and check microphone rejection and feedback at the performance position.

definition: Electrical energy transferred per unit time, averaged over a stated interval. It is the time average of instantaneous voltage times current. Into a fixed resistor it equals RMS voltage squared divided by resistance; waveform peaks and an amplifier’s continuous output rating are separate quantities.
example: Music averaging 40 watts into an ideal resistor can have peaks that demand substantially greater amplifier voltage.

definition: The part of a longitudinal sound wave where local pressure and density are above their ambient values. It alternates with rarefaction; the disturbance travels while individual air particles move back and forth near their resting positions.

The return of part of an incident sound wave from a boundary. The reflected fraction and direction depend on wavelength, incidence angle, surface geometry and material; other energy may be absorbed or transmitted.

A sound source extended mainly along a line. An ideal long line has approximately cylindrical spreading, with about three decibels of level loss per distance doubling; a finite loudspeaker array only approximates this over a frequency- and geometry-dependent region and eventually behaves differently.
example: Do not apply a three-decibel distance rule to every position or frequency around a real line array.
